But when the same model both produces the reasoning trace and extracts the formal constraint, the constraint inherits the trace's biases and errors \citep{huang2024selfcorrect, kambhampati2024position}.

\item \textbf{Oracle-Extraction Gap.} Oracle constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. The failure localizes to extraction quality, not the symbolic approach (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Effect.} SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone ($\sim$50--55\% SC accuracy). Above this range, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative. Below it, error amplification degrades accuracy. Three failure modes (Type~A, B, C) explain the regime boundaries (\S\ref{sec:main-results}, \S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).

The same LLM extracts structured first-order logic (FOL) constraints from each trace $t_i$ at a lower temperature $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$. While we prompt for FOL-style formalizations, the extracted constraints are predominantly ground propositional clauses without quantifiers, reflecting instruction-scale model capabilities. We define the \emph{extraction rate} as the fraction of traces yielding at least one parseable constraint. Traces with no valid constraints are excluded from MAX-SAT but still contribute answers to the candidate pool.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective across tasks without additional training.
It is also hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models, a pattern consistent across model families and reasoning tasks.
The plateau is consequential: test-time compute is the primary knob available to practitioners who cannot retrain or scale model parameters, and if additional samples stop helping, aggregation-based scaling faces a hard limit.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch between the independence assumption underlying majority voting and the correlated nature of same-model traces.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions of SC alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
Traces sampled from the same model carry correlated errors.
When most traces converge on the same (possibly wrong) answer, additional samples provide no new information, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct the shared bias.
Trained reward models \citep{lightman2024prm, wang2024mathshepherd} and diversity-aware sampling \citep{diverseaware2026} break this plateau by injecting external signal or controlling trace diversity, but require either trained verifiers or modifications to the sampling procedure.
A more fundamental question remains: can \emph{structured aggregation} over symbolic representations extract information from the same traces that majority voting cannot?
If symbolic representations capture logical relationships that natural language answers discard, aggregation over constraints could in principle recover signal that vote counting misses.

Recent neuro-symbolic methods suggest that formal reasoning can complement LLM generation.
Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} translate natural language problems into first-order logic (FOL) for external provers.
More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated FOL verifiers \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}.
These methods report gains on logical reasoning benchmarks, but each introduces components beyond the reasoning model itself: trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases.
A simpler question precedes these architectural extensions: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
If so, self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade to SC that requires no additional model, no training data, and no external prover.
Any LLM could be augmented with symbolic verification through a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver.
The appeal is practical: self-extraction scales with the base model, requires no domain-specific engineering, and preserves the simplicity that makes SC attractive in the first place.
Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which they succeed or fail.
This question motivates our study of Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}, which provides a formal lens for understanding when aggregation succeeds.
CJT states that if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority is correct with probability approaching 1 as $K$ grows \citep{austensmith1996}.
SC implicitly depends on this guarantee: when independence holds, more traces monotonically improve accuracy.
When it fails, as \citet{ladha1992correlated} show for correlated voters, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Same-model traces violate independence.
We measure inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa} and find values from 0.21 to 0.82 across our experimental conditions, yielding an effective sample size (Eff-$K$) of 1.20 to 3.63 for nominal $K = 12$ (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
In practical terms, 12 sampled traces from the same model carry the information of fewer than 4 independent opinions, and in the most correlated conditions, barely more than 1.
At Eff-$K \approx 1$, each additional trace is informationally redundant, and no aggregation method operating on those traces alone can escape the plateau.
Symbolic verification could in principle inject independent signal, because formal logic validity does not depend on the generative model.
But when the same model both produces the reasoning trace and extracts the formal constraint, the constraint inherits the trace's biases and errors \citep{huang2024selfcorrect, kambhampati2024position}.
Self-extracted constraints do not constitute an independent check; they are a reformulation of the same evidence.
We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}: the traces that produce constraints also determine their quality, so the constraints cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass SC.
Recent work has examined CJT violations in LLM ensembles \citep{lefort2024condorcet_llm}, but no prior study connects this theoretical framework to symbolic constraint extraction.
The distinction matters: symbolic constraints appear to introduce a qualitatively different information source (formal logic rather than natural language votes), yet our analysis shows that the extraction step collapses this apparent independence back into the shared model distribution.

We evaluate SICA across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}, StrategyQA \citep{geva2021strategyqa}), and more than 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Our evaluation spans instruction-tuned and reasoning-specialized model variants to ensure the findings are not artifacts of a single model family.
The core finding is that SICA effectiveness is regime-dependent, confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy.
Within this zone, Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds).
Outside it, three distinct failure modes emerge (\S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).
In Type~A conditions (SC $\geq$ 60\%), constraints exhibit confirmation bias and merely echo the majority answer; SICA provides no significant gain across all tested conditions ($N > 1{,}600$ combined).
In Type~C conditions (SC $\leq$ 40\%), predominantly incorrect traces produce noisy constraints that actively degrade accuracy ($-2.83$\,pp, $p < 0.01$).
In Type~B conditions, domains that resist formalization yield no useful signal regardless of model accuracy.

Oracle controls causally localize the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
Replacing self-extracted constraints with gold FOL annotations produces $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound when constraints are discriminative.
Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this oracle ceiling; the gap localizes to extraction quality, not solver limitations.
We test nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions (prompting, architecture, capability, verification, diversity, and filtering), and all fail to widen the Goldilocks zone (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
The bottleneck is structural: it cannot be resolved within the same-model self-extraction paradigm.
Sensitivity analysis provides further diagnostic evidence: SICA gain follows an inverted-U curve as a function of $K$ (peaking at $K = 12$), and the effect collapses entirely at temperature $T = 1.0$, where trace diversity drops below the threshold needed for constraint disagreement (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
These patterns confirm that SICA's benefit is fragile, dependent on a precise balance of trace diversity and extraction quality that same-model sampling rarely achieves.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence Bottleneck.} We formalize the SC plateau through the Condorcet Jury Theorem. Same-model traces yield Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ (Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.63$ for $K = 12$), quantifying why additional traces provide diminishing returns. Self-extracted symbolic constraints inherit this correlation and cannot supply independent signal (\S\ref{sec:condorcet}, \S\ref{sec:effective-k}).

\item \textbf{Oracle-Extraction Gap.} Oracle constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. The failure localizes to extraction quality, not the symbolic approach (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Effect.} SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone ($\sim$50--55\% SC accuracy). Above this range, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative. Below it, error amplification degrades accuracy. Three failure modes (Type~A, B, C) explain the regime boundaries (\S\ref{sec:main-results}, \S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).

\item \textbf{Structural Bottleneck Diagnosis.} Nine remediation strategies spanning prompting, architecture, capability, verification, diversity, and filtering all fail to widen the effective zone, confirming the independence bottleneck is inherent to same-model self-extraction. $K$/temperature sensitivity analysis and entropy-conditioned breakdowns provide practitioners with deployment diagnostics for predicting when symbolic aggregation can and cannot help (\S\ref{sec:remediation}, \S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought traces is the dominant test-time aggregation strategy for large language models (LLMs), but accuracy gains saturate as sample count grows. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) explains this plateau: same-model traces are correlated voters, so additional samples carry diminishing independent information. Symbolic constraints expressed in first-order logic (FOL) appear to offer a way forward, since formal validity is independent of the generative model. Yet when constraints are extracted by the same model that produces the traces, they inherit the traces' correlation structure. We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}. We study this bottleneck through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts FOL constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT. Evaluating six models (7B to 32B parameters) across four reasoning domains with over 2,400 instances and three-seed replication, we find that SICA gains are confined to a narrow accuracy regime around 50 to 55\% SC baseline. Outside this zone, constraints either echo the majority (confirmation bias) or amplify errors. Oracle controls with gold FOL annotations confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound, yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of the oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The bottleneck is structural: same-model self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass majority voting.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and over 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.21$--$0.82$, and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.63$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone of approximately 50--55\% SC accuracy, where Mistral-7B on FOLIO achieves $+4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ marks the inverted-U peak, and the effect collapses at $T = 1.0$.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:exp-setup}

We evaluate SICA against Self-Consistency (SC) across six instruction-tuned and reasoning-specialized models on four reasoning domains, with more than 2,400 evaluation instances.

\paragraph{Models.} Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen3-14B (non-thinking mode)~\citep{yang2024qwen25}, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3~\citep{jiang2023mistral}, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct~\citep{dubey2024llama3}, and QwQ-32B~\citep{qwen2024qwq}. Parameter counts range from 7B to 32B.

\paragraph{Datasets.} FOLIO~\citep{han2022folio} ($n=204$) provides formal logic problems with gold first-order logic (FOL) annotations for the oracle control (\S\ref{sec:oracle}). ProofWriter~\citep{tafjord2021proofwriter} ($n=600$) tests multi-step deductive reasoning at depth~5. LogiQA~\citep{liu2020logiqa} ($n=200$) evaluates logical reasoning from standardized examinations. StrategyQA~\citep{geva2021strategyqa} ($n=200$) covers commonsense multi-hop reasoning. GSM8K~\citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} ($n=30$) and AIME 2024 ($n=22$) serve as operating-regime probes for the degenerate case ($C_0 < 5\%$).

\paragraph{Parameters.} $K=12$ traces at sampling temperature $T=0.7$. Constraint extraction at $T_{\text{ext}}=0.3$ (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}). Z3~\citep{demoura2008z3} timeout: 10 seconds per problem. Penalty weight $\alpha = 0.5$ in all experiments.

\paragraph{Metrics.} Accuracy (\%), $\Delta = \text{SICA} - \text{SC}$ in percentage points (pp). Statistical significance via McNemar exact test at $\alpha = 0.05$; 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals from 10{,}000 resamples for datasets with $n \geq 200$.


\subsection{Main Results: A Regime-Dependent Effect}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reports accuracy across all model-dataset conditions sorted by SC baseline. SICA effectiveness depends sharply on the model's baseline accuracy regime, with a narrow Goldilocks zone as the only region of significant positive effect.

In the Goldilocks zone (SC $\sim$50--55\%), SICA provides significant gains on FOLIO. Qwen3-14B (SC $= 83.82\%$) represents a generational capability improvement yet produces $\Delta = +0.49$\,pp ($p > 0.05$).

\paragraph{Type C (SC $\leq$ $\sim$40\%): error amplification.} Mistral-7B on ProofWriter depth-5 ($n = 600$, SC $= 39.33\%$) shows $\Delta = -2.83$\,pp ($p = 0.0095$): SICA \emph{significantly hurts} performance. The oracle rows (bottom of Table~\ref{tab:main_results}) confirm that gold constraints yield $\Delta = +14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), establishing that the aggregation mechanism is sound when constraints are discriminative (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).

\subsection{Oracle Control: The Aggregation Mechanism Is Sound}
\label{sec:oracle}

Oracle variants replace self-extracted constraints with gold annotations: FOL formulas from FOLIO ($n = 204$) and domain-specific logic (DSL) programs from ProofWriter ($n = 600$). The oracle evaluates gold constraints against each candidate answer via Z3 directly; the scoring function (Eq.~\ref{eq:score}) remains unchanged. This design functions as a causal intervention on constraint quality while holding the aggregation mechanism constant.

Oracle-SICA achieves 89.71\% on FOLIO versus 75.49\% for SC ($\Delta = +14.22$\,pp, $p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$, McNemar $b = 29$, $c = 0$). Z3 agrees with gold labels on 95.1\% of FOLIO problems (194/204). On ProofWriter, Oracle-SICA reaches 86.67\% versus 75.17\% ($\Delta = +11.50$\,pp, $p = 9.21 \times 10^{-15}$), with Z3 gold agreement of 97.1\% (577/594). Relational subtypes benefit most: RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp and RelNoneg $+13.01$\,pp (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:pw_oracle_subtype}).

These results establish two conclusions. First, the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound: given discriminative constraints, it produces large and highly significant gains. Second, the gap between self-extraction and oracle performance quantifies the independence bottleneck. Mistral-7B's best self-extracted result ($+4.90$\,pp) captures only 34.5\% of the FOLIO oracle ceiling ($+14.22$\,pp). The remaining 65.5\% is lost to self-extraction quality. Section~\ref{sec:failure-modes} decomposes this loss into three distinct failure modes.


\subsection{Three-Seed Replication}
\label{sec:replication}

The Goldilocks result rests on Mistral-7B FOLIO performance, so we replicate with three random seeds to assess stability. All three runs use identical hyperparameters ($K = 12$, $T = 0.7$, $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$) on the full FOLIO evaluation set ($n = 204$).

Seed~42 produces $\Delta = +4.90$\,pp ($p = 0.013$, SC $= 54.41\%$). Seed~123 replicates both the direction and significance at $\Delta = +3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.039$, SC $= 53.92\%$). Seed~456 shows no effect ($\Delta = -0.49$\,pp, $p = 1.0$, SC $= 56.37\%$). Two of three seeds reach significance at $\alpha = 0.05$; the mean effect across seeds is $\Delta = +2.61$\,pp. The cross-seed mean does not reach significance (95\% CI includes zero with $n = 3$ seeds), consistent with the regime-boundary fragility that motivates our independence analysis.

The variance is informative. Seed~456 produces a slightly higher SC baseline (56.37\% vs.\ 53.92--54.41\%) and no SICA gain, consistent with the regime-dependence pattern: as SC rises toward the upper boundary of the Goldilocks zone, the improvement vanishes. Sampling noise at the regime boundary can push individual seeds across the transition, which makes the effect fragile by design rather than by accident. This seed-level sensitivity motivates the entropy-conditioned analysis in \S\ref{sec:entropy}, where per-problem answer entropy reveals that the aggregate $\Delta$ is driven by the high-entropy subpopulation within each run.


\subsection{Failure Mode Analysis}
\label{sec:failure-modes}

The regime-dependent pattern in Table~\ref{tab:main_results} reflects three distinct failure modes of self-extracted symbolic constraints.

\paragraph{Type A: confirmation bias (SC $\geq$ $\sim$60\%).} Strong models produce consistent reasoning traces, and constraints extracted from those traces mirror the answer distribution. When most constraints support the same candidate, MAX-SAT excludes few clauses ($|\mathcal{C}^{\setminus}| \approx 0$), the penalty term in Eq.~\ref{eq:score} vanishes, and the scoring function degenerates to weighted vote counting (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}). SICA and SC then produce identical predictions. The ablation in \S\ref{sec:ablation} confirms this empirically: on Qwen2.5-14B (FOLIO + ProofWriter, $n = 804$), MAX-SAT and count-only baselines agree on 803 of 804 predictions.

\paragraph{Type B: non-formalizable domains.} LogiQA problems require pragmatic and contextual reasoning that resists clean FOL formalization. Qwen2.5-14B on LogiQA achieves an extraction rate of 86.4\% (fraction of traces yielding at least one parseable constraint), but the resulting constraints have a contradiction rate of only 0.8\%: extracted formulas rarely conflict across traces, leaving MAX-SAT with no logical tension to exploit. Mistral-7B on LogiQA sits in the Goldilocks SC range (51.00\%) yet produces $\Delta = +0.50$\,pp ($p = 1.0$); Qwen2.5-14B on the same domain yields $\Delta = -0.50$\,pp ($p = 1.0$). Neither model benefits, confirming that the right accuracy regime is necessary but not sufficient when the domain resists formalization.

\paragraph{Type C: error amplification (SC $\leq$ $\sim$40\%).} When model accuracy is low, the majority of traces reach incorrect answers. Constraints extracted from wrong traces encode incorrect reasoning as formal rules. Z3 treats these rules as soft clauses with weight proportional to their frequency, so the solver preferentially satisfies the wrong constraints and penalizes traces that happen to reach the correct answer. Mistral-7B on ProofWriter ($\Delta = -2.83$\,pp, $p = 0.0095$) demonstrates this effect: SICA converts a weak positive signal in trace diversity into a net negative by formalizing the errors.

**Overall**: SICA=78.0%, SC=78.5%, Delta=-0.5pp, n=200

## Additional Stats

- **Avg majority fraction**: 0.913

| [1.25, 1.50) | 8 |
| [1.50, 1.75) | 2 |

Mean=0.290, Median=0.000, Std=0.435, Max=1.730

## Override Analysis

- **Low entropy**: 0 overrides (SICA never disagrees with SC)
- **Med entropy**: 1 override, all bad (SC right -> SICA wrong)
- **High entropy**: 2 overrides, 1 good + 1 bad = net zero

Total overrides: **3 out of 200** problems (1.5%)

## Cross-Experiment Comparison

| Metric | Qwen14B FOLIO-204 (exp-026) | Mistral-7B FOLIO-204 (exp-033) | Qwen14B LogiQA-200 (exp-038) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overall SICA | 85.3% | 70.1% | 78.0% |
| Overall SC | 84.8% | 67.2% | 78.5% |
| Overall Delta | +0.5pp | +2.9pp | -0.5pp |
| Low entropy n% | ~90% | 64.2% | 75.0% |
| Low entropy delta | +0.0pp | +0.0pp | +0.0pp |
| High entropy n% | 10.3% | 35.8% | 8.0% |
| High entropy delta | +4.8pp | +9.6pp | +0.0pp |
| Unanimous rate | - | - | 63.0% |

## Key Findings

1. **Low entropy = no difference**: Consistent with FOLIO findings. When SC votes are near-unanimous, SICA adds nothing (and correctly avoids overriding).

2. **High entropy provides no benefit on LogiQA**: Unlike FOLIO where high-entropy bins showed +4.8pp (Qwen) and +9.6pp (Mistral), LogiQA shows +0.0pp. Only 2 overrides in this bin, with 1 good and 1 bad canceling out.

3. **Extremely few overrides**: Only 3/200 (1.5%) problems have SICA != SC. On FOLIO, SICA overrode more frequently. This suggests the constraint extraction on LogiQA is less effective at producing discriminative signals.

4. **Mass distribution**: 75% low-entropy (between FOLIO-Mistral's 64% and FOLIO-Qwen's 90%). Only 8% high-entropy problems, a small pool where SICA could theoretically help.

5. **Net negative**: The single bad override in the medium-entropy bin accounts for the overall -0.5pp delta. SICA's constraint signal on LogiQA is too weak to overcome SC.

270	\section{Case Studies: Discordant Predictions}
271	\label{app:case-studies}
272	
273	Among 804 problems, SICA and SC agree on 773 (96.1\%). The 31 discordant cases comprise 16 SICA wins (SICA correct, SC wrong), 14 SC wins (SC correct, SICA wrong), and 1 where both select different wrong answers. All 31 occur at exact ties (entropy${=}1.0$, 6:6 vote split) or near-ties (entropy${\geq}0.9183$, 8:4 at most), since SICA can differ from SC only when constraint weights shift the majority away from SC's tiebreak choice. We present three representative cases that illustrate the mechanism behind capability trap failures.
274	
275	\paragraph{Case 1: SICA Wins (folio\_134, FOLIO).}
276	
277	\emph{Premises}: Some mammals have teeth. Platypus have no teeth. Platypus are mammals. Humans have teeth. \emph{Conclusion}: Humans are mammals. \emph{Gold}: Unknown.
278	
279	The premises state that \emph{some} mammals have teeth and that humans have teeth, but ``having teeth'' is not sufficient for ``being a mammal'' under open-world semantics. SC produces a 6:6 split (Unknown:6, True:6) and tiebreaks alphabetically to True (wrong). SICA extracts 7 constraints; MaxSAT excludes 1 constraint inconsistent with the rest, reducing the weighted score for True-voting traces and tipping the aggregation to Unknown (correct). The excluded constraint likely captured an incorrect inference step (e.g., affirming the consequent) present only in True-voting traces. While SICA succeeds here, the success is coincidental: the excluded constraint happens to anti-correlate with the correct answer.
280	
281	\paragraph{Case 2: SC Wins (ProofWriter-1066\_Q6, ProofWriter).}
282	
283	\emph{Key chain}: White(Bob)$\to$Round(Bob) [white things are round] $\to$ Young(Bob) [all round things are young]. \emph{Conclusion}: ``Bob is not young.'' \emph{Gold}: False (Bob IS young).
284	
285	SC produces a 6:6 split (False:6, True:6) and tiebreaks to False (correct). SICA extracts 17 constraints; MaxSAT excludes 2 that appear preferentially in False-voting traces. These excluded constraints likely captured correct intermediate derivations (e.g., \texttt{young\_bob == True}) that appeared only in traces completing the full deduction chain. By excluding them, MaxSAT removes evidence supporting the correct answer. SICA selects True (wrong). This case illustrates how self-extracted constraints can systematically mislead: correct reasoning steps become discriminative signals that the solver mistakenly penalizes.
286	
287	\paragraph{Case 3: Non-discriminative Constraints (ProofWriter-903\_Q6, ProofWriter).}
288	
289	\emph{Key chain}: Nice(Mouse)$\to$Cold(Mouse) [all nice people are cold] $\to$ Chases(Mouse,Mouse) [nice and cold $\to$ chase mouse]. \emph{Conclusion}: ``The mouse does not chase the mouse.'' \emph{Gold}: False.
290	
291	SC produces a 6:6 split (False:6, Unknown:6) and tiebreaks to False (correct). SICA extracts 44 constraints but excludes only 1 (2.3\%). The remaining 43 are domain facts and grounded rules (\texttt{nice\_mouse == True}, \texttt{Implies(nice\_mouse, cold\_mouse)}, etc.) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the final answer. Both False-voting and Unknown-voting traces share the same premises and grounded rules; they differ only in whether the trace completed the full derivation chain. The single excluded constraint carries negligible weight against 43 shared constraints, so SICA collapses to SC.
292	
293	\paragraph{Pattern.}
294	
295	These cases exemplify the general pattern across the 773 agreeing problems: the vast majority of extracted constraints encode shared domain structure rather than answer-specific reasoning, and MaxSAT aggregation degenerates to majority vote. Table~\ref{tab:case_summary} summarizes.

# exp-033 Analysis: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 SICA vs SC on FOLIO-204

## Experiment Config
- **Model**: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (vLLM)
- **Dataset**: FOLIO-204 (full validation set)
- **K**: 12, **T**: 0.7, **seed**: 42
- **Server**: westd-25068
- **Wall time**: 4744.9s (~79 min)
- **Status**: incomplete (198/204 problems, 97.1% coverage), process terminated mid-execution (no completion marker in log, log ends at HTTP requests). Summary section in JSON is stale snapshot from n=188; actual results array contains 198 entries.

## Key Metrics (n=198)

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **SICA accuracy** | 59.09% (117/198) |
| **SC accuracy** | 54.04% (107/198) |
| **Delta (SICA - SC)** | **+5.05pp** |
| Extraction rate | 97.10% |
| C0 (zero-constraint problems) | 1/198 (0.5%) |
| Contradiction rate | 3.52% |
| Problems with contradictions | 124/198 (62.6%) |
| Same answer (SICA = SC) | 181/198 (91.4%) |

## Statistical Significance

**McNemar's test (discordant pairs):**

| | SC correct | SC wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **SICA correct** | 105 | 12 |
| **SICA wrong** | 2 | 79 |

- Discordant pairs: sica_only=12, sc_only=2 (total=14)
- Chi-squared (uncorrected): (12-2)^2 / 14 = **7.14**, p = 0.0075
- Chi-squared (Yates corrected): (|12-2|-1)^2 / 14 = **5.79**, p ~ 0.016
- Exact binomial test (two-sided): P(X >= 12 | n=14, p=0.5) * 2 = **0.013**
- **Conclusion: statistically significant at p < 0.05 (all three tests)**

## Comparison with Prior Experiments

| Experiment | Model | Dataset | n | SC acc | SICA acc | Delta | Significant? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| exp-001 | Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct | FOLIO-204 | 204 | 74.51% | 74.75% | +0.25pp | No |
| exp-010 (pilot) | Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 | FOLIO-60 | 60 | ~53% | ~53% | 0pp | No |
| **exp-033** | **Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3** | **FOLIO-204** | **198** | **54.04%** | **59.09%** | **+5.05pp** | **Yes (p=0.013)** |

## Hypothesis Evaluation

**Original hypothesis**: Capability trap persists across model families. Mistral-7B should show delta ~ 0, confirming that weak models extract low-quality constraints that fail to improve over SC.

**Actual result**: SICA significantly outperforms SC by +5.05pp (p=0.013). This **contradicts** the capability trap hypothesis as stated.

## Interpretation

1. **SICA helps more on weak models**: Mistral-7B SC accuracy is low (54%) compared to Qwen2.5-14B (74.5%). When SC has low agreement/confidence, SICA's constraint-weighted voting provides additional discriminative signal that shifts answers in the right direction.

2. **Discordant pair asymmetry is strong**: 12 problems corrected by SICA vs only 2 lost. SICA is not randomly perturbing answers; it systematically improves on SC errors.

3. **Pilot inconsistency**: The pilot exp-010 (n=60) showed delta=0, but the full dataset shows +5.05pp. The pilot sample was likely unrepresentative, or the effect requires larger n to surface.

4. **Capability trap needs refinement**: The raw capability trap hypothesis ("weak model = bad constraints = no improvement") is too simplistic. The data suggests a more nuanced picture where SICA's benefit depends on the gap between SC agreement level and ground truth, not just constraint quality in isolation.

## Result Classification

The cross-family capability trap is NOT confirmed. SICA shows statistically significant improvement over SC on Mistral-7B, the weakest model tested so far. This complicates the paper narrative but strengthens the method's empirical case.

1	Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought traces is the dominant test-time aggregation strategy for large language models (LLMs), but accuracy gains saturate as sample count grows. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) explains this plateau: same-model traces are correlated voters, so additional samples carry diminishing independent information. Symbolic constraints expressed in first-order logic (FOL) appear to offer a way forward, since formal validity is independent of the generative model. Yet when constraints are extracted by the same model that produces the traces, they inherit the traces' correlation structure. We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}. We study this bottleneck through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts FOL constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT. Evaluating six models (7B to 32B parameters) across four reasoning domains with over 2,400 instances and three-seed replication, we find that SICA gains are confined to a narrow accuracy regime around 50 to 55\% SC baseline. Outside this zone, constraints either echo the majority (confirmation bias) or amplify errors. Oracle controls with gold FOL annotations confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound, yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of the oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The bottleneck is structural: same-model self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass majority voting.
